sections.h2: What is Peoria's history and layout?
sections.html:
Peoria was the earliest permanent European settlement in what became Illinois. French explorers built Fort Crevecoeur here in 1680, Fort Clark followed in 1813, and the town took the name Peoria when the county was organized in 1825. It became a village in 1835 and a city in 1845.

The city covers about 48 square miles of land, and its neighborhoods include Downtown, the East Bluff, the West Bluff, the Uplands, Moss-Bradley, North Valley, Northwest Peoria, the Heart of Peoria, University East, and the Glen Oak-Flanagan and Randolph-Roanoke historic districts. Several of those areas, such as Averyville and El Vista, began as separate unincorporated towns that the city absorbed, so a Peoria sale can look very different from one neighborhood to the next.

sections.h2: How big is the Peoria housing market, and who lives there?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau counted 113,150 residents in 2020 and estimated 110,920 for July 2025, a drop of 2.0 percent from the 2020 base. Pekin, across the river, has about 31,000.

Only 57.5 percent of units are owner-occupied, so a large landlord and investor base is part of the market, and the city has rules for properties that owners do not live in, covered below.

sections.h2: What jobs and hospitals drive demand in Peoria?
sections.html:
Health care leads. OSF HealthCare has been the top employer since 2021 and moved its headquarters into a renovated downtown building in 2022. It opened a $250 million cancer institute in February 2024. Carle Health completed its purchase of Methodist and Proctor hospitals from UnityPoint in 2023 and is the third-largest employer.

Industry still matters:

  • Caterpillar Tractor Co. was formed in 1925, kept its world headquarters in Peoria for over 110 years, and remains the second-biggest employer even though the headquarters moved to Deerfield after a late 2017 announcement.
  • Komatsu America builds off-highway trucks in Peoria and announced a new office building in September 2024.
  • Bradley University, Methodist College, the OSF St. Francis College of Nursing, the University of Illinois College of Medicine at Peoria and Illinois Central College's north campus are based in the city.

The hospitals cluster in a medical district near Interstate 74 and Knoxville Avenue, southeast of downtown.

sections.h2: Which roads and school districts matter for a Peoria address?
sections.html:
Interstate 74 runs through downtown and crosses the river on the Murray Baker Bridge. Interstate 474 forms a southern bypass, and Interstate 155 runs south from Morton toward Lincoln. Illinois Routes 6, 8, 29 and 40 and U.S. Route 150 serve the city itself.

Several school districts cover the city:

  • Peoria Public Schools District 150 serves most of it, with Richwoods, Manual and Peoria High School, the oldest high school in Illinois.
  • Dunlap Community Unit School District 323 serves the far north and northwest.
  • Pleasant Valley School District 62, Limestone Community High School District 310, Peoria Heights District 325 and Illinois Valley Central District 321 cover edge areas.

Because a few blocks can change a child's district, give buyers the district name that matches the address.

sections.h2: How does Peoria's weather affect older houses?
sections.html:
Peoria has a humid continental climate. Precipitation averages about 36 inches a year and snowfall about 26.3 inches. The recorded extremes run from minus 27 degrees in January 1884 to 113 degrees in July 1936, and the 1991 to 2020 normals put July afternoons near 86 degrees and January afternoons near 34.

Swings that wide are hard on older roofs, flashing, chimneys and basement walls. A buyer's inspector will ask how old the roof, chimney and basement walls are and when they were last repaired. Collect receipts and permit records before you list.

sections.h2: What must you do with a Peoria rental or vacant property?
sections.html:
The city requires registration of rental properties, vacant residential properties and any dwelling the owner does not live in. Owners renew by February 28 each year. A new registration is due within 30 days after closing or after the home becomes non-owner occupied.

Fees listed by the city:

  • Renewal for a single-family home is $75; a multi-family property pays $75 for the first unit and $20 for each additional unit.
  • New single-family registrations cost $75 from January 1 to September 30 and $50 from October 1 to December 31.
  • A late registration fee of $150 per property applies after February 28 or more than 30 days after purchase.

You can register as exempt when the property is vacant and for sale, with an MLS or other listing as proof, when it is in probate or estate settlement, when an immediate family member lives there, when it holds a city Mothball Permit, or when an owner-occupied home is temporarily vacant for up to six months. Owners who live outside Peoria, Tazewell and Woodford counties must appoint a local property manager. Tell the city if you sell or buy a property, and use the Change of Status form to deactivate a sold property's registration.

sections.h2: What does the Peoria transfer declaration require at closing?
sections.html:
The City of Peoria's real estate transfer declaration prints a tax of $2.50 per $1,000 of consideration or part thereof. It also asks you to check whether the property will be owner occupied or non-owner occupied. If the non-owner box is checked, section 5-522(a) of the city code requires the property to be registered as non-owner occupied at the time of closing.

The form lists exemptions, including deeds where the actual consideration is less than $100, tax deeds, deeds that only confirm or correct a prior recorded deed, and deeds to or from governmental bodies. The county side runs separately: Peoria County takes part in the state MyDec system, which allows the PTAX-203 to be submitted electronically before the deed is recorded. Ask your closing attorney or title company to prepare the city form with the county filing so nothing holds up the recording.

sections.h2: How can you sell a Peoria house fast?
sections.html:
With a median value of $156,200 and a large rental share, a house that needs work often sells to an investor. Those buyers pay cash, close on your schedule and buy as-is, while a listed sale usually means repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal.

  • Decide whether the house is owner occupied, vacant or rented, since that sets the registration steps.
  • Collect the deed, tax bills and any code notices.
  • Compare a cash offer to a listing by what you net after repairs and carrying costs.

faqs.q: How much is the City of Peoria real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: The city's transfer declaration prints $2.50 per $1,000 of consideration or part thereof. The form includes a list of exempt deed types. Ask your closing attorney to complete it with the PTAX-203 filed through the county.

faqs.q: Do I have to register a Peoria house I am selling?
faqs.a: Only if it is not owner occupied. Vacant homes listed for sale qualify for an exempt registration when you give the city an MLS or other listing as proof. After a sale, tell the city and use the Change of Status form to deactivate the registration.

faqs.q: When is Peoria's non-owner-occupied registration due?
faqs.a: Renewals are due every year by February 28, and new properties must be registered within 30 days after closing or after becoming non-owner occupied. A $150 late fee applies after those dates.

faqs.q: Which school district is my Peoria house in?
faqs.a: Most of Peoria is in District 150, but Dunlap District 323, Pleasant Valley District 62, Limestone District 310, Peoria Heights District 325 and Illinois Valley Central District 321 cover other parts. Check the address with the district before you list.

faqs.q: Is Peoria a good market for a quick cash sale?
faqs.a: A cash sale is an option for many houses. Only 57.5 percent of units are owner occupied, so investors and landlords are part of the buyer pool. Compare any offer against a listed sale after repairs, fees and carrying costs.
